title: Cow 412 — Holstein, 12 days fresh: off feed with a drop in yield
presentation: Second-lactation Holstein, calved twelve days ago. Milk yield down from 34 to 21 litres in three days, eating about half her ration, and the herdsman says her breath smells sweet.

stages.title: Examine the fresh cow
stages.briefing: BCS 3.5/5 at calving, now 3.0/5. HR 84 bpm, RR 30/min, temperature 38.5°C. Rumen contractions 1 per minute and weak. Faeces firm and scant. Uterine discharge non-odorous. No ping on left-side auscultation and percussion. Ketone smell on the breath. Milk 21 L, previously 34 L.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to a metabolic problem in the transition period?

options.label: Sweet ketone smell on the breath
options.detail: Acetone on expired air

options.label: Loss of half a body condition score in 12 days
options.detail: Rapid mobilisation of body fat

options.label: Reduced dry matter intake with a falling yield 12 days fresh
options.detail: The classic window for negative energy balance

options.label: No ping on left-side percussion
options.detail: Useful — it argues against a displaced abomasum

options.label: Non-odorous uterine discharge
options.detail: Makes metritis unlikely, but does not point to metabolism

stages.explanation: Twelve days fresh, dropping yield, eating half a ration and smelling of acetone is negative energy balance until proven otherwise. The absence of a ping and of a stinking discharge are worth recording because they take the two common concurrent diseases off the list — but they exclude rather than diagnose, and a cow can have ketosis and a displaced abomasum on the same day.

stages.title: Choose the cow-side tests
stages.briefing: You are on the farm with a hand-held meter, urine dipsticks and the option of sending blood away.

options.label: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate by hand-held meter
options.detail: The reference test for ketosis, cow-side

options.label: Urine ketone dipstick
options.detail: A quick screen, less specific than blood BHB

options.label: Serum calcium
options.detail: Subclinical hypocalcaemia travels with this

options.label: Liver enzymes — GGT and AST — with albumin
options.detail: Hepatic lipidosis grades the severity

options.label: Non-esterified fatty acids
options.detail: Quantifies the fat being mobilised

options.label: Bulk milk PCR for BVD
options.detail: A herd question, not an answer for this cow today

options.label: Abdominocentesis
options.detail: Not indicated with no evidence of peritonitis

stages.explanation: Blood BHB is the test that matters and it takes thirty seconds on a meter; the urine strip is a screen you use when you have no meter, because it lags and over-reads. Adding calcium and NEFA turns a single answer into a transition-period picture, and the liver panel tells you whether this cow is heading for fatty liver — which changes the prognosis, not just the treatment.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Blood BHB 3.4 mmol/L (ketosis >1.2). Urine ketones 3+. Calcium 1.9 mmol/L (ref 2.1–2.6). NEFA 1.1 mmol/L (raised). GGT 48 U/L, AST 160 U/L (both mildly raised), albumin 28 g/L (low). Glucose 2.1 mmol/L (low). Rumen fluid pH 6.8, protozoa sluggish. Herd data: eight of thirty-two fresh cows over the last month have had BHB above 1.2 mmol/L.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Clinical ketosis with hypoglycaemia
options.detail: BHB 3.4 mmol/L with glucose 2.1 mmol/L

options.label: Concurrent subclinical hypocalcaemia
options.detail: Calcium 1.9 mmol/L in a fresh cow

options.label: Early hepatic lipidosis
options.detail: Mildly raised liver enzymes with a low albumin

options.label: A herd-level transition problem, not one sick cow
options.detail: A quarter of fresh cows above the BHB threshold

options.label: Subacute ruminal acidosis is the primary problem
options.detail: Rumen pH 6.8 is normal

options.label: Left displaced abomasum is confirmed
options.detail: No ping, and nothing here images or implies it

stages.explanation: The individual diagnosis is straightforward; the herd number is the finding that earns the visit. Eight of thirty-two fresh cows over threshold means the dry-cow ration, feed space or body condition at drying-off is wrong, and treating this cow without saying so guarantees a return visit. The normal rumen pH is what stops you blaming acidosis, which is the reflex answer on a high-yielding unit.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: BHB 3.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.1 mmol/L, calcium 1.9 mmol/L, raised NEFA, mildly raised liver enzymes with low albumin, and a quarter of the fresh cows over the ketosis threshold.

options.label: Clinical type II ketosis with subclinical hypocalcaemia, on a herd transition problem
options.detail: The cow and the herd in one diagnosis

options.label: Subacute ruminal acidosis
options.detail: Rumen pH is normal

options.label: Left displaced abomasum
options.detail: No ping and no supporting finding

options.label: Metritis
options.detail: Non-odorous discharge, no fever

options.label: Simple hypocalcaemia (milk fever)
options.detail: Real but secondary; it does not explain a BHB of 3.4 mmol/L

stages.explanation: Type II ketosis — the fat-cow version arising from over-conditioning at calving — is treated with propylene glycol, glucose and calcium, and prevented by fixing the dry period. Naming the herd problem in the same sentence as the cow is what turns a treatment into a piece of veterinary work the farm actually benefits from.
